# Finding the First Paper {#sec-first-paper}

A literature search needs a starting point: one paper that is on topic. From that paper you can follow references and citations (@sec-citations). This chapter shows how we found ours and how we checked its bibliographic data.

## The first query

Our first search used a general web search engine with the query

```
"algebra" bookkeeping double-entry book filetype:pdf
```

The `filetype:pdf` part asks for PDF files, and all but one of the results we received were PDFs. Among the results was a PDF of @ellerman1985 on the author's own website, and a PDF of @ellerman2014 on arXiv. Both are by the same author. The abstract of @ellerman2014 describes bookkeeping in terms of a group, which matched our first question in @sec-question. We chose @ellerman2014 as the starting paper because it is the more recent of the two. A recent paper is a good start because its reference list can lead back to earlier work.

## One paper, several versions

A paper often exists in more than one version. @ellerman2014 has at least three records:

| Version | Identifier | Date |
| --- | --- | --- |
| arXiv preprint | arXiv:1407.1898 | 2014-07-07 |
| SSRN posting | DOI 10.2139/ssrn.2463442 | 2014 |
| Journal article in *Accounting Education*, vol. 23, no. 5, pp. 483–501 | DOI 10.1080/09639284.2014.949803 | 2014 |

The arXiv date comes from the arXiv API. The other two rows come from the records registered with Crossref, which we queried through its public API. When you cite a paper, cite the published version, and record the preprint as a freely readable copy.

## Checking the bibliographic data

A search result is a pointer to a paper, and the details it shows can be incomplete. Before a reference enters the bibliography of this book, we check it against a record kept by the publisher or by a registry.

1. **arXiv.** The arXiv API returns the title, authors, abstract, subject category, and first submission date of a preprint. We queried it with `au:Ellerman AND abs:bookkeeping` and received exactly one record, arXiv:1407.1898.
2. **Crossref.** We sent each journal article and conference paper in this book's bibliography, as free text, to Crossref's public API (`api.crossref.org/works` with the `query.bibliographic` parameter). It returned the closest registered records with their DOI, journal, volume, issue, pages, and date.

The Crossref result is only a candidate. Compare it with the reference you are checking: same authors, same title, same year. @sec-limits shows a case where the best match was a different record.

## Exercises

1. Find a starting paper for your topic. Explain why you chose it over the other results.
2. Find every version of your starting paper (preprint, journal article, repository copy). Record each version's identifier and date in your log.
3. Send the citation of your starting paper to the Crossref API and compare the returned record with what you have. Note any differences.
